title: The full ocean
hookLine: as rivers flow into the full ocean without disturbing it, so desires flow into the one at peace (Bhagavad Gita 2.70)
tomorrow: the good news finally comes. so why does your stomach drop?

cards: Stand on a beach long enough and it's strange: rivers pour into the sea all day, every day, and the sea stays where it is. So, yesterday's question: why doesn't it overflow? Krishna's answer in the Gita isn't about water.
It's about wanting: the new phone, the next trip, the one more thing. And it's the picture he leaves Arjuna with as the chapter closes.

teach.b: Here's the verse, paraphrased. As waters flow into the ocean, which is full and stays unmoved, so desires flow into the one at peace. That person reaches peace, not the one who chases desires.
Notice what the ocean doesn't do.
It doesn't stop the rivers. It doesn't build a wall at every mouth. The rivers keep coming; the ocean is already full, so they don't push it around.
Then Krishna finishes the portrait of yesterday's steady one.
The person who lets go of desires and moves through life without craving, free of "I" and "mine", reaches peace.
And the chapter's last verse names it: this is the state of Brahman, and reaching it, one is no longer deluded.
That's the teaching Hindus take from the close of chapter two: peace isn't getting every want filled, and it isn't wanting nothing.

It's being full already, so the wants arrive and settle. And the story doesn't stop there. The next chapter opens with Arjuna pushing back: if understanding is better than action, why urge me into this terrible work?
The ocean picture doesn't end his questions. It gathers three days of the Gita. Evenness in the work.
Steady in sorrow and in joy. And now full, so the rivers can come.

how: Hindus read the close of Bhagavad Gita chapter two (2.70–72) as the summit of its portrait of the person of steady wisdom; the ocean verse is recited and taught on its own.

o: a mind already full, so incoming wants don't move it
a mind emptied of every single wish and feeling
the sea of rebirth that a soul must sail across

games.q: the rivers and the sea: tap the pairs.
p: what the peaceful one lets go

s: in Gita 2.70, no desires come to the person at peace
desires still flow in, like rivers; the full ocean isn't disturbed.
the Gita's second chapter closes on the state of Brahman
reaching it, Krishna says, one is no longer deluded.
the ocean stays calm because it blocks the rivers
the rivers keep pouring in; it's already full.

games.q: your friend just got a raise and suddenly wants a bigger apartment, a new car and a trip, all this month. what would the full ocean say?
o: notice the wants arriving; you don't have to chase each one to be at peace.
chase them all now, while you can; peace comes once they're all done.
turn down the raise, since wanting anything at all is the real problem.
games.why: the rivers keep flowing in, and the full ocean isn't moved. peace isn't chasing every want, or having none.

practice: Take a glass of water, or wait for your next sip. Before you drink, notice the wanting; then drink slowly, and notice the wanting settle, like a river reaching the sea. Sit with the fullness after.

wordCard.voice: The full ocean: Krishna's picture of the one at peace, who takes in every river of desire and isn't moved.

orig.note: Sanskrit: ocean, the image in Bhagavad Gita 2.70.

carryVoice: Carry this: the full ocean, where the rivers arrive and settle. Thirty days into the old books.
